messages.content: I have a few chickens that survived a sudden death outbreak. Can I take them to market?

No, you must not move, sell or give any bird after a Newcastle disease outbreak. First isolate every surviving bird from the sick ones. Then burn or bury all dead birds and the soiled litter. Disinfect the house thoroughly. Finally vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in drinking water or as eye-drops and follow the vaccination schedule. If you need help, contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary immediately.
Many of my chickens died all at once and the rest look fine. Should I still take the healthy ones to the market?

No, you must not move, sell or give any bird after a sudden mass death. Burn or bury the dead birds and any soiled litter. Disinfect the house. Vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in drinking water or as eye-drops and repeat as scheduled. See the veterinary service or village livestock auxiliary right away.
My chickens are coughing and then several died suddenly; can I still transport the remaining birds?

No, you must not move, sell or give any bird after those signs. Isolate every surviving bird from the sick ones. Burn or bury the dead birds and any contaminated litter. Disinfect the house. Vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in drinking water or as eye-drops and keep to the vaccination schedule. Contact the veterinary service or village livestock auxiliary immediately.
How should I handle a flock infected with Newcastle disease virus?

Newcastle disease virus requires you to keep all birds on the farm; do not move, sell or gift any bird. First isolate every surviving bird from the sick ones. Then burn or bury dead birds and the soiled litter and disinfect the house. After that vaccinate the flock with the La Sota (or B1) strain in drinking water or as eye-drops, repeating on the recommended schedule. For assistance, see the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary right away.
Can I take sick chickens to market?

No, you must not move, sell or give any bird that shows signs of Newcastle disease. First isolate every surviving bird from the sick ones to stop spread. Then burn or bury all dead birds and any soiled litter, and disinfect the house thoroughly. After cleaning, vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain by adding it to the drinking water or applying it as eye-drops, and keep to the repeat schedule. Finally, contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary right away for further help.
My birds have sudden deaths, so it must be fowl pox, I will just burn the dead and move the rest to market.

It is not fowl pox, it is Newcastle disease. Newcastle causes older birds to die suddenly in large numbers, while fowl pox shows scabs or lesions and progresses more slowly. Because it is Newcastle, you must not move, sell or give any bird. Isolate every surviving bird from the sick ones, then burn or bury all dead birds and any soiled litter and disinfect the house. Vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in drinking water or as eye-drops and repeat on schedule. See the veterinary service or village livestock auxiliary immediately.
I have some chickens that I want to take to the market, but I'm not sure if it's safe.
Are many of your birds dying suddenly?
Yes, several died at once and the others look fine.

You are dealing with Newcastle disease, which causes sudden mass deaths in older birds. Isolate every surviving bird from the sick ones and do NOT move, sell or gift any bird. Burn or bury the dead birds and any soiled litter, then disinfect the house thoroughly. Vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as an eye-drop and repeat the vaccination on the recommended schedule. Contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary immediately for help.
What should I do to manage cassava bacterial blight in my field?

Use cuttings only from healthy plants. Remove and destroy any plants that show angular water-soaked spots, wilting young leaves or shoot die-back. After each plant you pull, disinfect your tools before moving to the next one. Plant a resistant cassava variety in the cleared area. Rotate the plot to a new location after harvesting. For clean resistant cuttings you can go to ITRA or a registered producer, and to be sure of the disease you can ask ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.
My cassava leaves have angular water-soaked spots and the young leaves are wilting, what does this mean?

Those signs are typical of cassava bacterial blight. Cuttings must come only from plants that look healthy, so do not take any from the affected ones. Pull out the plants that have the spots and wilting and destroy them. Clean your cutting tools with a disinfectant before you work on the next plant. Plant a resistant variety in the space you free up. If you need clean resistant cuttings, visit ITRA or a registered producer, and you can ask ICAT to check the disease.
I see some of my cassava stems oozing a gummy substance, should I be worried?

Gum exuding from stems is another symptom of cassava bacterial blight. Do not use cuttings from any plant that shows this gum. Remove those plants and destroy them completely. Disinfect your tools between each plant you handle. Use only cuttings taken from healthy plants for the next planting. Choose a resistant cassava variety and rotate the plot after harvest. For clean resistant cuttings you can obtain them from ITRA or a registered producer, and ICAT can help confirm the disease if you are unsure.
How do I treat Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. manihotis in my cassava crop?

The disease caused by Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. manihotis is called cassava bacterial blight. Start by using cuttings only from plants that look healthy. Pull out and destroy any plants that have angular water-soaked spots, wilting young leaves, shoot die-back or gum on stems. After each plant, disinfect your tools before moving to the next one. Plant a resistant cassava variety in the cleared area and rotate the plot for the next cycle. For clean resistant cuttings you can go to ITRA or a registered producer, and you can ask ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.
blight spots wilting shoots what now

The disease is cassava bacterial blight. Use cuttings only from healthy plants. First, walk through your field and select stems that show no angular water-soaked spots, no wilting of young leaves, and no gum on the stems. Second, pull out any plant that has those symptoms and destroy it completely. Third, clean each cutting tool with a disinfectant before moving to the next plant to stop spread by tools. Fourth, plant a resistant cassava variety in the cleared area and rotate the plot to reduce future risk. For clean resistant cuttings and confirmation, go to ITRA or a registered producer and ask ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.
It is cassava mosaic, I will take cuttings from the healthy side

It is not cassava mosaic, it is bacterial blight. Mosaic shows yellow mottling and leaf deformation without wilting, while blight gives angular water-soaked spots, wilting of young leaves, shoot die-back and sometimes gum on stems. Remove and destroy any plant with the spots, disinfect all tools between plants, and use cuttings only from plants that have no symptoms at all. Plant a resistant variety and rotate the plot. Have ICAT confirm the diagnosis and get clean resistant cuttings from ITRA or a registered producer.
When does the rainy season start for blight spread?

The disease spreads most during the rainy season when rain splash can move the bacterium. To limit spread, use cuttings only from healthy plants, remove and destroy any affected plants, disinfect tools between each cutting, and plant a resistant variety while rotating the plot. I cannot give you the exact date the rainy season starts, but you can ask the local agricultural office or weather service for that information. For clean resistant cuttings and diagnosis confirmation, visit ITRA or a registered producer and see ICAT.
My cassava leaves are looking strange and some parts of the plant are dying.
Are the spots on the leaves angular and water-soaked with wilting of young leaves?
Yes, the spots are angular, water-soaked and the young leaves are wilting.

You are dealing with cassava bacterial blight. Use cuttings only from healthy plants to avoid spreading the disease. Remove and destroy any affected plants to stop further infection. Disinfect your tools between each plant to prevent contamination. Plant a resistant variety and rotate the plot to reduce future risk. See ITRA or a registered producer for clean resistant cuttings and ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.

Use cuttings only from healthy plants. First walk through your field and select stems that have no angular water-soaked spots, no wilting young leaves and no gum on the stems. Cut those stems and discard any plant showing those symptoms. After cutting, disinfect your tools before moving to the next plant to avoid spreading the bacterium. Remove and destroy any affected plants you find in the field. Plant a resistant cassava variety in the cleared area and rotate the plot to reduce disease build-up. If you need clean cuttings, get them from ITRA or a registered producer, and you can ask ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.
My cassava leaves have angular water-soaked spots and the young leaves are wilting, should I still use those stems for planting?

No, do not use those stems. Remove and destroy the affected plants immediately. Disinfect your cutting tools before you work on any other plant. Choose only stems from plants that show no spots, no wilting and no gum on the stems. Plant a resistant variety in the cleaned area and rotate the plot. For clean cuttings you can obtain them from ITRA or a registered producer, and ICAT can help confirm the disease.

which cuttings are safe to use

Only cuttings from healthy plants are safe. Look for leaves without angular water-soaked spots, no wilting of young leaves, and no gum on stems. If any of those signs appear, do not take cuttings from that plant. Choose plants that show normal green foliage and no disease symptoms. After cutting, keep tools clean and disinfect them between plants. Plant resistant varieties and rotate the plot to reduce future risk. For clean cuttings you can consult ITRA or a registered producer.
why must I only use healthy cuttings

Using only healthy cuttings stops the spread of bacterial blight. The disease moves through diseased stems, contaminated tools, and rain splash. If you take cuttings from a plant with angular water-soaked spots, wilting leaves or gum on stems, you carry the bacterium Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. manihotis to the new field. For confirmation you can visit ICAT.
my leaves have angular spots, is that cassava mosaic

It is not cassava mosaic, it is bacterial blight. Cassava mosaic shows yellow mottling and leaf deformation without wilting, while bacterial blight shows angular water-soaked spots, wilting of young leaves and sometimes gum on stems. Check your leaves: if you see wilting and angular spots, it is bacterial blight. Remove and destroy those plants, disinfect tools, and plant a resistant variety. For a proper diagnosis you can ask ICAT.

Do the leaves have angular water-soaked spots and are the young leaves wilting?
Yes, the leaves have those spots and the new leaves are wilting.

The problem is bacterial blight, so use cuttings only from healthy plants because moving diseased stems, contaminated tools, and rain splash spreads the disease. First, remove and destroy all affected plants to stop the source of infection. Then disinfect your tools between each plant to avoid carrying the bacterium. Next, plant a resistant cassava variety and rotate the plot to reduce future risk. Finally, obtain clean resistant cuttings from ITRA or a registered producer and ask ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.
How should I cut and plant cassava cuttings?

Cut healthy stems that are 6-12 months old into pieces 15-25 cm long with at least 5 nodes, then plant them within 3 days. Bury two-thirds of each cutting slanted, node-tops up, never lay flat. Space the plants 1 m by 1 m, which gives about 10,000 plants per hectare. If you inter-crop with maize, plant the cassava within 2 weeks of the maize. Weed the field 2-3 times while the plants are small. For clean improved cuttings, see ITRA or a registered producer.
I have a small field and some cassava stems that are about a year old. I want to start a new planting and I also grow some maize nearby. What steps should I follow?

Use the stems that are 6-12 months old and cut them into lengths of 15-25 cm, making sure each piece has at least 5 nodes, then plant the cuttings within 3 days. Bury two-thirds of each cutting slanted with the node-tops up, never lay it flat. Plant the cuttings 1 m apart in rows and columns, giving about 10,000 plants per hectare. Because you grow maize, plant the cassava within 2 weeks of the maize. Weed the area 2-3 times while the cassava plants are still small. For clean improved cuttings, contact ITRA or a registered producer.

Yes, I have healthy stems of that age.

Plant in March in the south or in May-June in the north after a good rain. If you have had mosaic problems, obtain clean improved cuttings from ITRA or a registered producer.
My cowpea field has poor pod set. What should I do to improve it?

Use a resistant improved cowpea variety that matures in 55 to 75 days and sow it when the rains are strong, usually from mid-June to early July. Spray an approved insecticide three times during flowering: first when flower buds appear at 30-35 days after sowing, second ten days later, and third ten days after that, always at the labelled rate. Because insects come back in waves, a single spray will not protect the whole crop. Before each spray, ask ICAT for the current approved product and the exact dose to use.
I see damaged and dropped flowers and some pods look bored. What can I do?

Plant a resistant improved cowpea variety that matures in 55-75 days and sow it when the rains are strong, around mid-June to early July. Weed early, with the first weeding about two weeks after sowing, to keep the field clean. Apply an approved insecticide three times during flowering: first at 30-35 days when flower buds appear, then ten days later, and again ten days after that, using the label rate. This schedule attacks the waves of thrips, pod borers and aphids that cause the damage. Check with ICAT for the current approved product and the exact dose before each spray.
My cowpea plants have many insects on the flowers and the pods are being chewed. How should I manage this?

Choose a resistant improved cowpea variety that reaches maturity in 55-75 days and sow it when the rains are strong, typically mid-June to early July. Perform the first weeding about two weeks after sowing to reduce weed competition. Spray an approved insecticide three times around flowering: first when flower buds appear at 30-35 days, second ten days later, and third ten days after that, following the label rate. The three sprays cover the waves of flower thrips, pod borers and aphids that attack the crop. Before spraying, contact ICAT to get the current approved product and the exact dose.
How do I control Maruca pod borers and aphids in my cowpea field?

The everyday name is pod borers and aphids, and you should use a resistant improved cowpea variety that matures in 55-75 days, sowing it when the rains are strong, from mid-June to early July. Weed early, doing the first weeding about two weeks after sowing. Spray an approved insecticide three times during flowering: first at 30-35 days when flower buds appear, then ten days later, and again ten days after that, at the labelled rate. This schedule targets the waves of insects that damage flowers and pods. Ask ICAT for the current approved product and the exact dose before each application.
why are my pods not setting

Poor pod set is caused by thrips, pod borers and aphids attacking flowers and pods. my cowpea has damaged pods, must be storage weevils, so just treat after harvest

It is not storage weevils, it is flower thrips, pod borers and aphids that cause damaged, dropped flowers and bored pods in the field. Storage weevils appear after harvest and are dealt with ash, oil or an approved insecticide, while the field insects attack during flowering. To control the field pests, sow a resistant improved 55-75 day variety when rains are strong, weed early about two weeks after sowing, and spray three times around flowering at 30-35 days, then 10 days later, then another 10 days later, using the approved product at the labelled rate. The guidance is to spray three times around flowering: first at 30-35 days when flower buds appear, second 10 days later, third 10 days after that, using an approved product at the labelled rate. I cannot give you the exact amount per hectare, but you should obtain the current approved product and exact dose from ICAT before spraying.
My cowpea plants are not making many pods and I see some bugs on them.
Which insects are you seeing on the flowers or pods?
I see tiny insects on the buds and some larger moth-like bugs on the pods.

The poor pod set is caused by flower thrips, pod borers such as Maruca, and aphids that damage flowers and bored pods. Sow a resistant improved 55-75 day cowpea variety when the rains are strong, usually from mid-June to early July. Weed early, doing the first weeding about two weeks after sowing. Spray three times around flowering: first spray at 30-35 days when flower buds appear, second spray ten days later, and third spray ten days after the second, using an approved product at the labelled rate. My groundnut leaves have dark round spots and they are turning yellow and falling off early.

It is groundnut leaf spot caused by Cercospora fungi. Rotate groundnut with cereals so you do not grow it on the same land year after year. Use a tolerant variety and clear or bury the old groundnut residues. Harvest on time because a weakened crop drops its pods. For resistant varieties or advice on fungicide use, see ICAT.
What should I do if I suspect maize stalk borer in my field?

It is maize stalk borer. While the plants are young, put a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each leaf funnel; this treats about 1,500 to 2,000 plants per kilogram. Repeat the application every 8 to 10 days while the crop is still young. Never use neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the plant, always mix it with an inert carrier. Also rotate or intercrop the field with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. If a large block is attacked at once, go to ICAT quickly for approved control.
My maize plants have window-pane holes in the whorl leaves and the central shoot looks dead while the outer leaves are still green. What is happening?

Those signs are caused by maize stalk borer. While the plants are still young, drop a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each leaf funnel; one kilogram covers about 1,500 to 2,000 plants. Do not apply neem powder alone because the oil will scorch the plant; always use the sand or clay carrier. After you harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and rotate or intercrop with a legume like cowpea or soybean. If many plants are affected at once, contact ICAT quickly for approved control.
I see a dead central shoot in my maize but the outer leaves are still alive. Could this be a pest problem?

A dead-heart with still-green outer leaves is typical of maize stalk borer. While the crop is young, place a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each leaf funnel; one kilogram treats roughly 1,500 to 2,000 plants. Repeat the treatment every 8 to 10 days during the young stage. Never use neem powder by itself because the oil can scorch the plant; always mix it with the inert carrier. After harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and practice rotation or intercropping with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. For a large, suddenly attacked block, see ICAT quickly for approved control.
How do I manage Busseola fusca infestations in my maize?

Busseola fusca is the maize stalk borer. While the plants are young, put a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each leaf funnel; one kilogram covers about 1,500 to 2,000 plants. Apply this mixture every 8 to 10 days while the crop remains young. Do not apply neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the plant; always use the sand or clay carrier. After harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and rotate or intercrop with a legume like cowpea or soybean. If a large area is attacked at once, go to ICAT quickly for approved control.

my maize has dead-heart so it must be maize streak virus, right?

It is not maize streak virus. Dead-heart with window-pane holes in the whorl is caused by the stalk borer, not the virus that only gives pale streaks along veins. The borer makes tunnels and the dead-heart, while the virus does not produce tunnels or dead-heart. Because it is a borer, you must put a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each funnel while the plants are young, repeat every eight to ten days, and never use neem powder alone. how many grams of neem powder should I put per plant?

How does the maize stalk borer survive in old stalks and what should I do after harvest?

The stalk borer can live in the old stalks left in the field after harvest. After you finish harvesting, destroy the old stalks or bury them deep so the larvae cannot survive. Then plant a legume such as cowpea or soybean in the same area to break the pest cycle. Rotate or intercrop with the legume immediately after the old stalks are removed. If a large block of your field is attacked at once, go to ICAT quickly for approved control. I cannot give you a specific date for these actions.

My pepper seedlings are falling over and the stems are breaking right at the soil line.

Your seedlings are likely suffering from damping-off caused by nursery soil fungi that thrive in overly wet beds. Keep the bed evenly moist but never soggy, and stop watering late in the evening so moisture does not stay overnight. Use seed that has been treated with a fungicide-insecticide coating and sow it at a spacing that is not too thick, which reduces the chance of infection. If the disease keeps spreading, visit ICAT for an approved nursery drench and the proper application rate.
seedlings collapse soil line what do?

Keep the bed evenly moist but never soggy, and stop watering late in the evening so moisture does not stay overnight. My pepper seedlings are collapsing at the soil line, I think it's transplant shock. Should I just wait for them to recover?

It is not transplant shock, it is damping-off caused by nursery soil fungi that thrive in too-wet beds. The two are told apart by the stage: transplant shock appears on older plants after moving, while damping-off shows seedlings topple and collapse right at the soil line in the nursery. Because it is damping-off, keep the bed evenly moist but never soggy and avoid watering late in the evening. Sow treated seed with a fungicide-insecticide coat and do not sow too thickly. Remove any collapsed seedlings, improve drainage and airflow in the bed. If the problem keeps spreading, go to ICAT for an approved nursery drench and rate.
What exact amount of nursery drench should I use to stop the damping-off in my pepper seedlings?

Use an approved nursery drench when damping-off keeps spreading, and follow the rate given for the product you choose. The drench should be applied after you have kept the bed evenly moist but not soggy, stopped watering late in the evening, sowed treated seed, and removed collapsed seedlings while improving drainage and airflow. I cannot give you the exact amount to use, and you should ask ICAT for the approved drench and its correct rate for your situation.

How can I prevent rice blast in my rice field?

Rice blast is prevented by managing nitrogen and seed. First, stop over-applying nitrogen; split urea applications and never exceed the recommended dose. Second, treat the seed you will sow next season with a Fongorene-type product at 6 g per kg of seed. Third, if you already have a severe outbreak, apply an approved benomyl-type fungicide at about 500 g per hectare, improve drainage and airflow, and plant a tolerant variety. How can I prevent bloat in my cattle and goats when the pasture becomes very lush?

My corn has little holes that look like window panes on the whorl leaves and the middle shoot seems dead while the outer leaves stay green. What is it?

My sow fell sick and died yesterday, what must I do with her body?

You have to get rid of the dead pig by either burying it deep in the ground or burning it completely, and you must never try to sell or eat that sick pig. First, keep all the remaining pigs locked inside their pen and stop any movement of pigs off or onto the farm. Do not let any visitors approach the enclosure. Clean the pen thoroughly and place a footbath at the entrance for anyone who enters. Boil any kitchen leftovers before offering them to the pigs. Remember there is no cure or vaccine for African swine fever. You must inform the veterinary service right away.

My chickens are showing little raised bumps on their faces and combs, what is happening?

The raised bumps on the face and comb are the dry form of fowl pox. First, keep those chickens apart from the healthy birds. Then give the affected chickens extra feed and fresh water while the mild dry form runs its course. After that, eliminate mosquito breeding by removing any standing water and keeping the area clean. Next, vaccinate all of your chickens against fowl pox to stop the disease spreading. If you notice any wet-form signs, you should contact the veterinary service.
I found some of my hens with wart-like scabs on their wattles, how should I deal with it?

Wart-like scabs on the wattles are a sign of the dry form of fowl pox. Separate the scabbed hens from the rest of the flock immediately. Provide those hens with additional feed and clean water while the dry form passes. Then reduce mosquito numbers by clearing standing water and keeping the surroundings tidy. Afterward, vaccinate the entire flock against fowl pox to prevent further cases. For any wet-form symptoms or further help, see the veterinary service.
My coop is near a ditch that holds water after rain and I think mosquitoes are making my chickens sick. What can I do?

Mosquitoes breeding in standing water help spread fowl pox, so you must eliminate any puddles around the coop. First, separate any chickens that show raised, wart-like scabs on their combs, wattles or face from the healthy birds. Then give the isolated birds extra feed and clean water while the dry form of fowl pox runs its mild course. After that, drain or fill any standing water and keep the area around the coop tidy to cut down mosquito numbers. When the affected chickens recover, arrange vaccination for the whole flock against fowl pox. For any assistance, especially with the wet form, see the veterinary service.
My chickens just lost many birds in one day, but a few are still alive. Can I sell the survivors at the market?

You must not move, sell or give any chicken after a Newcastle disease outbreak. First separate every surviving chicken from the sick ones. Then burn or bury all dead chickens together with any contaminated litter. After that, clean and disinfect the coop thoroughly. Finally give the flock the La Sota or B1 vaccine in the drinking water or as eye-drops and repeat according to the schedule. If you need assistance, contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary right away.
Several of my hens died suddenly and the rest look okay, is it safe to take the healthy ones to the market?

No, you cannot transport any chicken after a Newcastle disease episode. Begin by isolating each surviving chicken away from the infected birds. Next, burn or bury the dead chickens and any soiled bedding. Then disinfect the housing area completely. Afterwards vaccinate the entire flock with the La Sota or B1 strain using drinking water or eye-drops, following the recommended schedule. You should see the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary immediately for help.

Finally, vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 vaccine in the water or as eye-drops, repeating as scheduled. My rice seedlings are getting sick, could it be from the seed I used?

Rice blast can be carried on seed, so you must treat the seed before sowing. First, avoid applying too much nitrogen by splitting urea and staying within the recommended dose. Then treat the seed you will sow next season with a Fongorene-type product at 6 g per kg of seed. If the disease is already severe, use an approved benomyl-type fungicide at about 500 g per hectare, improve drainage and airflow, and plant a tolerant variety. For the current approved fungicide and exact rate, go to ICAT.

My bull looks swollen on the left side and stopped eating after we moved him to the new wet pasture, what must I do?

The bull is suffering from bloat and you must keep roughage in the diet to avoid the problem. Get the bull up and walking while holding his head up so he can belch. Give a small amount of vegetable or mineral oil by mouth to break the froth and let the gas escape. Call the veterinary service right away because this is an emergency. You should see the veterinary service immediately.
The goat I take to the field today has a tight drum-like swelling on its left flank and is breathing heavily, what are the steps?

The goat is experiencing bloat and you should always keep roughage in the diet to prevent it. Move the goat and keep its head raised to help it release gas. Drench a little vegetable or mineral oil by mouth to break the froth inside the rumen. Contact the veterinary service without delay as this can be fatal quickly. You should see the veterinary service immediately.

The tomato leaves in my garden are yellow and curling upward, and I get almost no fruit. How should I treat these plants?

Rogue out the badly affected tomato plants right away. Begin by identifying all tomato plants that display upward curling, yellow leaves, stunted bushy growth and poor fruit set. Remove each identified plant from the garden and destroy it to stop further spread. Then keep the garden clean and act early to control any whitefly present, the vector of tomato yellow leaf curl virus. Plant a resistant tomato variety for your next crop. For help with whitefly management and resistant varieties, see ICAT.
